opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the simplest way to put it is that proteins are the machines of biology. Almost everything that happens in your cells, whether it's turning food into energy, copying DNA, sensing light in your eye, or fighting off an infection, is done by proteins. And the remarkable thing is that the genome gives us these proteins as a one-dimensional string of amino acids, but that's not how they do their job. They fold up into these very precise three-dimensional shapes, and it's the shape that determines what they do.

So if you want to understand a protein mechanistically, not just "this gene is associated with this disease," but *why*, then you really want to see it. You want to see where the active site is, how a mutation might disrupt a binding pocket, how two proteins fit together. It's the difference between knowing the parts list of an engine and actually having the blueprint.

And historically, getting that blueprint has been brutally hard. With X-ray crystallography, you have to express the protein, purify it, and then coax it into forming a crystal, which is often more art than science. People have spent years, entire PhDs, on a single structure, and sometimes it just never crystallizes. Cryo-EM has changed a lot of that, NMR has its place, but it's still expensive and slow, on the order of months to years per structure.

The reason people are willing to pay that cost is that the payoff is enormous. A structure can tell you how a drug binds, it can suggest how to design a better one, it can explain a disease mechanism that was a mystery for decades. Structural biologists have built up the Protein Data Bank over fifty-odd years, and that collective effort is honestly what made something like AlphaFold possible in the first place. We were standing on the shoulders of a huge amount of very painstaking experimental work.

So for me, the motivation for working on prediction was never that experiments don't matter. It was that there's this enormous gap between the number of protein sequences we know, hundreds of millions, and the number of structures we've solved, a couple hundred thousand. If computation can help close that gap, even approximately, then biologists get to ask questions they couldn't ask before, and they can focus their experimental effort on the really hard, interesting cases.

r001.rationale: The response says seeing a protein’s structure can explain why a disease-associated gene matters and show how a mutation might disrupt a binding pocket, conveying how the change contributes mechanistically to disease.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says people have spent entire PhDs on a single structure and sometimes the protein never crystallizes.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that structure is really the bridge between sequence and function. You have this genome, this string of letters, and it's enormously informative but also strangely mute. It tells you what the protein is made of, but it doesn't tell you what it does. And proteins do things because of their shape. An enzyme has a pocket that a particular molecule fits into. An antibody recognizes its target because of a surface that's complementary. Two proteins interact because they have faces that fit together. So when you know the structure, you suddenly have a way of reasoning about the mechanism, rather than just cataloguing that something happens.

And historically that knowledge was extraordinarily expensive. A single structure might be a PhD, might be years of work, might be a grant. You'd be purifying the protein, trying to get it to crystallize, which is almost an art form, and then collecting diffraction data at a synchrotron. And people did that, tens of thousands of times over decades, because the payoff was so large. If you understand how a protein works, you can start to think about how to design a drug against it, or how a mutation causes disease, or how you might engineer it to do something new.

I think the thing that struck me, coming into the field, was that the experimentalists were right about the value and the cost was just a historical accident of what tools we had. There was nothing fundamental saying the structure had to be hard to get. The information was in the sequence and in the evolutionary record. So the question that really motivated us was: can we get the same answer, or something close to it, for a fraction of the effort? Because if you can, you don't just make the existing experiments cheaper, you change what questions people are willing to ask. You go from asking about one protein you care deeply about to asking about every protein in an organism, and that's a qualitatively different kind of biology.

r001.rationale: The response says structures can help explain how a mutation causes disease, but it does not describe locating a disease-associated genetic change on the protein structure.

r002.rationale: It says solving a structure might take a PhD and involve trying to crystallize the protein, but does not say a researcher can spend the entire PhD without succeeding.

astra-6.text:
Well, a protein’s structure tells you a tremendous amount about how it works. Proteins are these remarkable molecular machines: they catalyze reactions, transmit signals, transport things, and give cells their shape. And all of that depends on how a chain of amino acids folds into a three-dimensional object.

If you know the structure, you can start asking very concrete questions. Why does this mutation disrupt its function? Where might a drug bind? How does it interact with another protein? You go from knowing that something is involved in a biological process to having a physical picture of what it might actually be doing.

Structure doesn’t answer every question—proteins move, and their environment matters—but it gives you an extraordinarily powerful starting point. That’s why people have been willing to spend years determining a single structure: it can unlock a whole programme of experiments.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, proteins are the little machines that make biology work. They carry out chemical reactions, transmit signals, move things around inside cells. And a lot of what they can do depends on their three-dimensional shape. You can know the sequence of a protein—the list of amino acids—and still have very little idea of how it actually works.

A structure gives you a way to start asking much more precise questions. Why does this protein bind that molecule? Why does a mutation disrupt its function? Could you design a drug that changes what it does? It doesn’t answer all of those questions on its own, because proteins move and interact with their environment. But it gives you an incredibly powerful starting point. That’s why people will spend years trying to determine one structure: it can unlock an enormous amount of biology.
